q: Unless the contract provides otherwise, the rates quoted by a contractor for the items of a work are treated as inclusive of:

options.A: Only the cost of the labour employed directly on those items
options.B: Only the cost of the materials incorporated in those items
options.C: All leads and lifts involved in bringing the materials to the place of use and executing the items at the site
options.D: The cost of the work excluding the cost of water and power used at the site in every case

e: Unless the contract provides otherwise, a contractor's quoted rates are inclusive of all leads and lifts involved in bringing materials to the place of use and executing the items at site. Separate payment for ordinary lead and lift is not admissible over and above the item rate.

q: The 'mode of measurement' referred to in a works contract lays down:

options.A: The instrument with which the Engineer will check the levels of the work
options.B: The period after which the measurements once recorded may be corrected
options.C: The order in which the several items of a bill are to be arranged
options.D: The manner in which each item of work is to be measured for payment, such as the unit of measurement and the deductions, if any, to be made

e: The mode of measurement in a works contract lays down how each item is to be measured for payment, including the unit of measurement and the deductions to be made. It ensures uniform measurement and billing of items across contracts.

q: In reckoning the areas of a building, the 'circulation area' of a floor means:

options.A: The area of the verandahs, corridors, passages, staircases and similar spaces which serve for movement within the floor
options.B: The area occupied by the walls and columns standing on the floor
options.C: The usable floor area of all the rooms situated on the floor
options.D: The area of the open terrace and balcony attached to the floor

e: Circulation area of a floor is the area of verandahs, corridors, passages, staircases and similar spaces used for movement within the floor. It is distinct from the usable carpet area of rooms and from the area occupied by walls.

q: Works are executed by the Railways as deposit works for outside bodies on the principle that:

options.A: The Railways earn a commercial profit on such works, like a private contractor
options.B: The Railways recover only the cost of the work together with the prescribed departmental charges, without any element of profit
options.C: The cost of such works is shared equally between the Railways and the body concerned
options.D: The departmental charges recovered on such works are treated as a subsidy to the body concerned

e: Deposit works are executed by the Railways for outside bodies on a no-profit basis. The Railways recover only the cost of the work plus the prescribed departmental charges, unlike a private contractor who works for commercial profit.

q: Railway land which is no longer required for railway purposes is ordinarily dealt with by:

options.A: Selling it to private parties by negotiation at a price fixed by the division
options.B: Allowing the staff in occupation of the adjoining quarters to retain it permanently
options.C: Relinquishing it to the State Government, following the prescribed procedure
options.D: Leasing it out permanently for commercial development without any approval

e: Railway land no longer required for railway purposes is ordinarily relinquished to the State Government following the prescribed procedure. It is not sold by the division by private negotiation or permanently leased out without approval.

q: The amount realised by the sale of railway land is treated in the Railway accounts as:

options.A: A part of the sundry earnings of the Railway for the year
options.B: A receipt of the Stores Department towards its sale of surplus materials
options.C: A fund kept apart for the purchase of land for future works
options.D: A capital receipt, credited to Capital in reduction of the capital-at-charge

e: The amount realised by sale of railway land is a capital receipt. It is credited to Capital in reduction of the capital-at-charge, and is not treated as sundry earnings or as a stores receipt.

q: In the estimate of a building work, the provision for internal water supply and sanitary installations, and for internal electrification of the building, is ordinarily made:

options.A: As a percentage of the estimated cost of the building (civil) work
options.B: At a fixed lump sum for every building, whatever its size
options.C: Only after the building is completed, from the actual bills of the agencies
options.D: By charging the cost to the maintenance grant of the following year

e: In a building estimate, provision for internal water supply and sanitary installations and for internal electrification is ordinarily made as a percentage of the estimated cost of the civil work of the building. This is the standard estimating practice for such services.

q: Under a contract governed by the General Conditions of Contract for Services, the staff engaged on the work by the service provider:

options.A: Become the employees of the Railways for the period of the contract
options.B: Remain the employees of the service provider alone, the contract creating no employer-employee relationship between them and the Railways
options.C: Are entitled to absorption in railway service on completion of the contract
options.D: Are paid their wages directly by the Railways in all cases

e: Under a services contract governed by the GCC for Services, the provider's staff remain the employees of the service provider alone. The contract creates no employer-employee relationship between them and the Railways, and they have no claim to absorption in railway service.

q: A 'combined footing' is provided in the foundation of a building when:

options.A: The soil is so weak that the whole building has to rest on a raft
options.B: The load from a wall has to be carried across an underground drain
options.C: Two columns stand so close together, or a column stands so close to the boundary, that their separate footings would overlap, and a common footing is provided for them
options.D: The depth of the foundation has to be taken below the water table of the area

e: A combined footing is provided when two columns stand so close, or a column stands so close to a boundary, that separate footings would overlap. A common footing then carries both columns.

q: A 'friction pile' used in the foundation of a structure derives its load-carrying capacity mainly from:

options.A: The resistance offered by a hard stratum on which the toe of the pile rests
options.B: The weight of the concrete with which the pile is filled
options.C: The grip of the cap provided at the top of the pile on the structure above
options.D: The friction developed between the surface of the pile and the surrounding soil along its length

e: A friction pile carries its load mainly through the friction developed between its surface and the surrounding soil along its length. It does not depend on resting its toe on a hard stratum, which is the principle of an end-bearing pile.

q: A reconnaissance survey carried out for a proposed new railway line is primarily intended to:

options.A: Prepare the final land plans and schedules for acquisition of land
options.B: Examine the general character of the country and the possible routes, so that the promising alignment or alignments can be selected for further detailed survey
options.C: Work out the detailed estimate of the line for sanction by the competent authority
options.D: Fix the exact locations of stations, bridges and culverts on the final alignment

e: A reconnaissance survey examines the general character of the country and the possible routes for a proposed line. Its purpose is to select the promising alignment or alignments for further detailed survey, not to prepare land plans or the detailed estimate.

q: A preliminary survey of a proposed new railway line, as distinguished from the reconnaissance survey, is carried out in order to:

options.A: Merely identify, from maps and aerial photographs, the routes that appear possible
options.B: Open the line for the public carriage of passengers after inspection
options.C: Collect detailed field data along the selected alignment, such as levels, soil conditions and crossings, needed for preparing the approximate estimate and the project report
options.D: Demarcate the land finally acquired for the line by fixing boundary pillars

e: A preliminary survey collects detailed field data along the selected alignment, such as levels, soil conditions and crossings. This data is needed for preparing the approximate estimate and the project report, going well beyond the map study of reconnaissance.

q: 'Segregation' in connection with fresh concrete placed in a work refers to:

options.A: The separation of the constituents of the concrete, such as the coarse aggregate separating from the mortar, during handling and placing
options.B: The stiffening of concrete after its initial set has begun
options.C: The development of fine cracks on the surface of hardened concrete due to drying
options.D: The bleeding of excess water from the concrete to its surface

e: Segregation is the separation of the constituents of fresh concrete, such as coarse aggregate separating from the mortar, during handling, transport and placing. It produces weak, honeycombed concrete and must be avoided.

q: 'Bleeding' of freshly placed concrete refers to:

options.A: The appearance of hair cracks on the surface of the concrete after curing
options.B: The loss of cement from the surface of the concrete due to rain
options.C: The separation of coarse aggregate from the mortar during transport
options.D: The appearance of water on the surface of the concrete after placing and compaction, as the solid particles settle down

e: Bleeding is the appearance of water on the surface of freshly placed and compacted concrete as the solid particles settle down. It is different from segregation, which is the separation of coarse aggregate from mortar.

q: The 'soundness' of cement used in a work refers to its property of:

options.A: Gaining strength rapidly within the first seven days of curing
options.B: Resisting the chemical action of sulphates present in the soil
options.C: Retaining its volume after setting, without delayed expansion or disintegration
options.D: Requiring only a low water-cement ratio for full hydration

e: Soundness of cement is its property of retaining its volume after setting, without delayed expansion or disintegration. Unsound cement, usually from excess free lime or magnesia, expands later and cracks the concrete or mortar.

q: An accelerating admixture (accelerator) added to a concrete mix serves to:

options.A: Delay the setting of the concrete so that it can be transported over long distances
options.B: Speed up the setting and early hardening of the concrete
options.C: Improve the workability of the concrete without adding extra water
options.D: Entrain microscopic air bubbles in the concrete to resist frost action

e: An accelerating admixture speeds up the setting and early hardening of concrete. It is useful in cold weather and where early strength or early removal of formwork is required, the opposite of a retarder.

q: In brickwork, 'Flemish bond' is a bond in which:

options.A: Headers and stretchers are laid alternately in every course of the wall
options.B: All the bricks in a course are laid as stretchers only
options.C: All the bricks in a course are laid as headers only
options.D: Header courses and stretcher courses are laid alternately along the height of the wall

e: In Flemish bond, headers and stretchers are laid alternately in every course of the wall. Alternate header and stretcher courses along the height is English bond, not Flemish bond.

q: A 'header' in brickwork is a brick which is laid:

options.A: Vertically in a course, with its long face exposed on the wall face
options.B: At the corner of a wall to maintain the bond between two faces
options.C: Cut to half its length for use next to a quoin header
options.D: Across the thickness of the wall, so that its short end face is exposed on the face of the wall

e: A header is a brick laid across the thickness of the wall, so that its short end face shows on the face of the wall. A brick laid lengthwise showing its long face is a stretcher.

q: A 'through stone' provided in stone masonry work is a stone which:

options.A: Is dressed to a wedge shape for use in the ring of an arch
options.B: Extends through the whole thickness of the wall and ties its two faces together
options.C: Is laid at the base of a wall to distribute the load on the foundation
options.D: Forms the topmost course of a parapet wall

e: A through stone extends through the whole thickness of a stone masonry wall. It ties the two faces of the wall together and prevents them from separating or bulging.

q: 'Pointing' carried out on masonry work consists of:

options.A: Applying a plaster coat over the whole face of the masonry wall
options.B: Filling the joints of the masonry with lime concrete before plastering
options.C: Finishing the exposed mortar joints of the masonry with a richer and denser mortar, to protect the joints and improve the appearance
options.D: Grouting the cavities inside a masonry wall with cement slurry

e: Pointing is the finishing of the exposed mortar joints of masonry with a richer, denser mortar. It protects the joints from weathering and improves the appearance, without plastering the whole wall face.

q: 'Grouting' in connection with masonry or foundation work means:

options.A: Injecting fluid cement mortar into the joints, cracks or voids of the structure so as to fill them and strengthen or seal the structure
options.B: Spreading a thin layer of mortar over a surface before laying the next course
options.C: Filling the space behind a retaining wall with dry stone packing
options.D: Applying a waterproof coating over the finished surface of a structure

e: Grouting is injecting fluid cement mortar into the joints, cracks or voids of a structure under pressure. It fills the voids so as to strengthen or seal the structure, as in foundation and masonry consolidation work.

q: A 'raft' (mat) foundation is adopted for a structure when the load is spread by means of:

options.A: A series of deep piles driven down to a hard stratum
options.B: Isolated pad footings provided under each column of the structure
options.C: A stepped masonry footing widened in successive courses
options.D: One thick reinforced concrete slab covering the entire area under the structure

e: A raft or mat foundation is one thick reinforced concrete slab covering the entire area under the structure. It spreads the total load over the whole area and is used where soil bearing capacity is low or settlements must be evened out.

q: An 'end-bearing pile' used in a foundation carries the load imposed on it mainly by:

options.A: The friction developed between the surface of the pile and the surrounding soil
options.B: Transferring the load through its tip to a firm stratum on which the tip rests
options.C: Spreading the load over the soil immediately below the pile cap
options.D: The adhesion of the soil to the sides of the pile near its top

e: An end-bearing pile transfers its load through its tip to a firm stratum on which the tip rests. This is the opposite of a friction pile, which relies on skin friction along its length.

q: A 'grillage foundation' provided under a heavy column consists of:

options.A: Tiers of steel beams embedded in concrete, which distribute the concentrated load of the column over a wider area of soil
options.B: A network of timber baulks laid directly on the ground under the column
options.C: A ring of short piles driven around the base of the column
options.D: A mass concrete block cast in steps below the column base

e: A grillage foundation consists of tiers of steel beams embedded in concrete under a heavy column. The tiers spread the concentrated column load over a progressively wider area of soil.

q: The 'safe bearing capacity' of the soil at the site of a foundation is:

options.A: The load at which the soil finally fails by shear
options.B: The weight of the soil removed from the foundation pit per unit area
options.C: The maximum load per unit area which the soil can safely support without shear failure or excessive settlement
options.D: The load per unit area imposed by the lightest structure the soil can carry

e: The safe bearing capacity is the maximum load per unit area the soil can safely support without shear failure or excessive settlement. It is the ultimate bearing capacity divided by a suitable factor of safety.

q: A 'cofferdam' used in connection with the foundation of a bridge in a river is:

options.A: A permanent protective apron laid around the pier foundation to resist scour
options.B: A temporary enclosure built in the water and pumped dry, so that the foundation work can be carried out in the dry
options.C: A floating platform from which the boring for the foundation is carried out
options.D: A masonry wall built across the river to divert its flow permanently

e: A cofferdam is a temporary enclosure built in water and pumped dry. It allows the foundation work for a bridge pier to be carried out in the dry and is removed after the work; it is not a permanent protection work.

q: 'Scaffolding' provided during the construction or repair of a building is:

options.A: The temporary support given to an unsafe wall to prevent its collapse
options.B: The framework of timber or steel which supports the formwork of a slab
options.C: The permanent steel staging provided inside a workshop for repairs
options.D: A temporary platform or framework erected to support workmen and materials at the required height

e: Scaffolding is a temporary platform or framework erected to support workmen and materials at the required height during construction or repair. Support to formwork is centering or shuttering, and support to an unsafe structure is shoring.

q: 'Shoring' provided to a structure means:

options.A: Giving temporary support to an unsafe or unstable structure, or to a structure being altered, so as to prevent its collapse
options.B: Strengthening the foundation of a structure by deepening it
options.C: Providing a temporary platform for workmen working at a height
options.D: Supporting the formwork of an arch until the mortar has set

e: Shoring is the temporary support given to an unsafe or unstable structure, or one being altered, to prevent its collapse. It supports the structure itself, unlike scaffolding which supports workmen and materials.

q: 'Underpinning' of an existing structure means the work of:

options.A: Providing additional bracing to the roof trusses of the structure
options.B: Waterproofing the walls of the structure below ground level
options.C: Strengthening or deepening the foundation of the structure, generally to carry additional load or to arrest settlement
options.D: Replacing the decayed wooden members of the structure with new ones

e: Underpinning is strengthening or deepening the foundation of an existing structure. It is done to carry additional load, to arrest settlement, or to allow deeper excavation nearby.

q: 'Seasoning' of timber before it is used in a work consists of:

options.A: Treating the timber with preservatives to protect it against white ants
options.B: Reducing the moisture content of the timber by drying, so that it gains strength and does not warp or shrink in use
options.C: Sawing the timber logs into scantlings of the required sizes
options.D: Polishing the surface of the timber to give it a finished appearance

e: Seasoning of timber is reducing its moisture content by drying before use. Properly seasoned timber gains strength and does not warp, shrink or crack in service; it is distinct from preservative treatment against termites.

q: The 'dead load' for which a structure such as a bridge or a building is designed is:

options.A: The load of the trains or vehicles that pass over the structure
options.B: The load exerted by wind pressure on the structure
options.C: The load of the workmen and materials present during construction
options.D: The weight of the structure itself and of its permanent components

e: Dead load is the weight of the structure itself and of its permanent components, such as girders, deck, ballast and track fixed on it. Moving trains are live load, and wind and construction loads are separate load cases.

q: The 'live load' for which a railway bridge is designed is:

options.A: The moving load of the trains that pass over the bridge
options.B: The weight of the girders and other members of the bridge itself
options.C: The pressure exerted by flood water on the piers of the bridge
options.D: The load of the ballast and track laid permanently on the bridge

e: Live load on a railway bridge is the moving load of the trains passing over it. The weight of the bridge itself, ballast and track is dead load, and flood pressure is a separate hydraulic load.

q: The 'clear span' of a girder or beam in a structure is:

options.A: The distance between the centres of its bearings on the two supports
options.B: The total length of the girder as fabricated, including the portions resting on the supports
options.C: The clear distance between the inner faces of the two supports
options.D: The distance between the outer faces of the two abutments of the bridge

e: Clear span is the clear distance between the inner faces of the two supports of a girder or beam. The distance between centres of bearings is the effective span, and the total fabricated length is longer still.

q: A 'plate girder' used in a railway bridge is a girder which is:

options.A: Cast in one piece with a hollow rectangular section
options.B: Built up of a web plate with flange plates or angles riveted, bolted or welded to it
options.C: Formed of members arranged in triangular panels with open webs
options.D: Made of rolled steel joists placed side by side without a web plate

e: A plate girder is built up of a web plate with flange plates or angles riveted, bolted or welded to it. A girder of triangular open-web members is a truss, not a plate girder.

q: A 'gusset plate' in a steel truss is the plate which:

options.A: Connects the members meeting at a joint of the truss, the members being fastened to it
options.B: Is fixed under the bearing of the truss to distribute the load on the abutment
options.C: Ties the two top chords of the truss together across the bridge
options.D: Strengthens the web of a plate girder against buckling

e: A gusset plate is the plate at a joint of a steel truss to which all the members meeting at that joint are fastened. It connects the members and transfers their forces through the joint.

q: A 'strut' in a framed structure is a member which is subjected mainly to:

options.A: Bending across its length
options.B: Twisting about its own axis
options.C: Tension along its length
options.D: Compression along its length

e: A strut is a structural member subjected mainly to compression along its length, such as a compression member in a truss or bracing. A member mainly in tension along its length is a tie.

q: A 'catch-water drain' provided in connection with a railway cutting is a drain which is:

options.A: Provided along the toe of an embankment to drain away water from its base
options.B: Dug along the top of the cutting on the uphill side, to intercept the surface water flowing towards the cutting and lead it away
options.C: Provided under the track in the cutting to lower the water table below the formation
options.D: Cut across the slope of the cutting at intervals to discharge rain water

e: A catch-water drain is dug along the top of a cutting on the uphill side. It intercepts surface water flowing towards the cutting and leads it away, so that the water does not flow down and erode the cutting slopes.

q: The side drains provided longitudinally in a railway cutting serve to:

options.A: Irrigate the land adjoining the railway boundary
options.B: Carry the water supply required for the steam locomotives
options.C: Collect the water flowing from the slopes and the formation of the cutting and convey it to a suitable outlet
options.D: Prevent trespassers from entering the railway land

e: Longitudinal side drains in a cutting collect the water flowing from its slopes and formation and convey it to a suitable outlet. Proper drainage of the cutting keeps the formation dry and stable.

q: 'Settlement' of a railway embankment refers to:

options.A: The gradual sinking down of the embankment, due to the compaction of the filling and the yielding of the ground below it
options.B: The washing away of the slopes of the embankment by rain water
options.C: The sliding of a mass of earth down the slope of the embankment
options.D: The growth of vegetation on the slopes of the embankment

e: Settlement of an embankment is its gradual sinking down due to compaction of the filling and yielding of the ground below. It differs from a slip, which is the sliding of a mass of earth down the slope.

q: A 'slip' which occurs in a railway embankment or cutting is:

options.A: A crack which develops across the top of the embankment
options.B: The scouring of the toe of the embankment by a stream
options.C: The settlement of the embankment uniformly over a length
options.D: The sliding down of a mass of earth from the slope, on account of failure of the slope

e: A slip is the sliding down of a mass of earth from the slope of an embankment or cutting due to failure of the slope. It is a slope failure, not uniform settlement, a crack, or scour of the toe.

q: In track work, a 'suspended joint' is a rail joint which is situated:

options.A: Directly over a sleeper, which supports it from below
options.B: Between two sleepers, instead of directly over a sleeper
options.C: At the end of a long welded rail panel
options.D: On a bridge, where the rails rest on the girders

e: A suspended joint is a rail joint located between two sleepers rather than directly over a sleeper. The joint is thus suspended in the ballast-supported span instead of resting on a joint sleeper.

q: The 'throw of the switch' in a turnout is:

options.A: The distance between the two running rails at the heel of the switch
options.B: The length of the tongue rail from its toe to its heel
options.C: The distance through which the tongue rail moves at its toe when the switch is operated from one position to the other
options.D: The gap left between the tongue rail and the stock rail for the flange of the wheel

e: The throw of the switch is the distance through which the tongue rail moves at its toe when the switch is operated from one position to the other. It is a movement at the toe, not the length of the tongue rail or the gauge at the heel.

q: The 'ballast cushion' in a railway track refers to:

options.A: The depth or thickness of the ballast provided below the bottom of the sleeper
options.B: The ballast heaped above the top of the sleeper at its ends
options.C: The layer of sand spread over the formation before the ballast is laid
options.D: The extra ballast stocked along the track for maintenance purposes

e: Ballast cushion is the depth or thickness of ballast provided below the bottom of the sleeper. Adequate cushion distributes the load on the formation and is a key element of track strength and drainage.

q: The 'ruling gradient' of a railway section is the gradient which:

options.A: Is provided in station yards to ensure drainage of the yard
options.B: Is the easiest gradient available anywhere in the section
options.C: Can be negotiated by a train by virtue of its momentum alone
options.D: Is the steepest gradient in the section and determines the maximum load that an engine can haul over the section

e: The ruling gradient is the steepest gradient in a section and determines the maximum load an engine can haul over that section. Trains are loaded to what the engine can take over this gradient.

q: In survey and levelling work, the 'reduced level' (RL) of a point is:

options.A: The reading obtained on the levelling staff held at that point
options.B: The height or elevation of that point above or below an assumed datum
options.C: The horizontal distance of that point from the start of the survey
options.D: The difference in level between that point and the next point surveyed

e: The reduced level of a point is its height or elevation above or below an assumed datum. It is the computed elevation, not the staff reading itself, which is only an observation used to derive it.

q: 'Consolidation' of the soil under a railway embankment refers to:

options.A: The compaction of the soil by rolling it in layers during construction
options.B: The increase in the density of the soil due to the passage of trains
options.C: The gradual squeezing out of water from a saturated clay soil under sustained load, resulting in a decrease in its volume
options.D: The cementing together of soil particles by natural agencies over time

e: Consolidation is the gradual squeezing out of water from a saturated clay soil under sustained load, causing a decrease in its volume. It is a time-dependent process, distinct from compaction by rolling during construction.

q: The 'dado' provided in a room of a building is:

options.A: A washable or protective finish applied to the lower portion of the internal wall above the skirting
options.B: The recess formed in a wall for fixing a cupboard
options.C: The beam provided over a wide opening in the wall of the room
options.D: The sunshade projected over the windows of the room

e: The dado is a washable or protective finish applied to the lower portion of the internal wall above the skirting. It protects the wall in areas subject to splashing or wear, such as bathrooms and corridors.

q: The 'sill' of a window in a building is:

options.A: The vertical member fixed at the side of the window opening
options.B: The horizontal member at the top of the window frame
options.C: The iron grill fixed outside the window for protection
options.D: The horizontal member or slab at the bottom of the window opening, on which the frame rests

e: The sill of a window is the horizontal member or slab at the bottom of the window opening, on which the frame rests. The vertical side member is the jamb and the top member is the head or lintel level.

q: The 'scrap value' of an asset at the end of its useful life is:

options.A: The value at which the asset stands in the books of account at that time
options.B: The amount that can be realised by dismantling the asset and selling its material as scrap
options.C: The cost of replacing the asset by a new asset of the same capacity
options.D: The value of the asset if it is transferred to another railway for further use

e: Scrap value is the amount realisable at the end of an asset's useful life by dismantling it and selling its material as scrap. It differs from book value, which is cost less depreciation, and from replacement cost.

q: The 'book value' of an asset appearing in the accounts of a Railway is:

options.A: The market price at which the asset could be sold at that time
options.B: The original cost of the asset, without any deduction for wear and tear
options.C: The original cost of the asset less the depreciation charged on it up to that time
options.D: The assessed value of the asset for the purpose of insurance

e: Book value of an asset is its original cost less the depreciation charged on it up to that time. It is an accounting value, not the current market price or the insured value of the asset.

q: An 'anticipatory breach' of a contract takes place when:

options.A: Before the time fixed for performance, one party to the contract declares that he will not perform his part, or renders himself unable to perform it
options.B: The performance of the contract becomes impossible due to an event beyond the control of the parties
options.C: A party performs the contract only partly and the other party accepts the part performance
options.D: The parties to the contract agree to substitute a new contract in place of the old one

e: Anticipatory breach occurs when, before the time fixed for performance, a party declares he will not perform his part of the contract or renders himself unable to perform it. The other party may then treat the contract as broken without waiting for the due date.

q: Under the principle of mitigation of damages for breach of a contract, the party who suffers from the breach:

options.A: Is entitled to recover the entire loss claimed by him, whether avoidable or not
options.B: Must take reasonable steps to minimise his loss, and cannot recover the loss which he could have so avoided
options.C: Is required to give the defaulting party a further opportunity to perform the contract
options.D: Can claim damages only after obtaining the permission of the Engineer

e: Under the mitigation principle, the party suffering from a breach must take reasonable steps to minimise his loss. He cannot recover loss which he could have avoided by such reasonable steps, under the Indian Contract Act principles applied in works contracts.

q: 'Mutation' in connection with land acquired for a railway work means:

options.A: The conversion of the acquired land from agricultural to non-agricultural use
options.B: The demarcation of the acquired land on the ground by boundary stones
options.C: The payment of compensation to the owners of the acquired land
options.D: The entry of the acquired land in the revenue records in the name of the Railways

e: Mutation is the entry of acquired land in the revenue records in the name of the Railways. It records the change of ownership in the State revenue records after acquisition and payment of compensation.

q: A 'caution order' issued in connection with works on or near a running line is:

options.A: An order directing the contractor to suspend the work until further instructions
options.B: A notice served on the contractor for his slow progress on the work
options.C: A written intimation to the drivers of trains about a temporary speed restriction or obstruction ahead, so that trains are run with caution over the affected portion
options.D: An order imposing a penalty on the contractor for defective work

e: A caution order is a written intimation to train drivers about a temporary speed restriction or obstruction ahead, arising from works on or near the running line. Trains are run with caution over the affected portion.

q: An imprest held by an engineering official for meeting petty works expenditure is 'recouped' when:

options.A: On an account of the amounts spent out of it being rendered, the amount so spent is reimbursed, restoring the imprest to its fixed amount
options.B: The unspent balance of the imprest is deposited back into the cash office at the end of the year
options.C: The imprest holder is permitted to enhance the amount of the imprest permanently
options.D: The imprest is converted into a temporary advance in the name of another official

e: An imprest is recouped when, on an account of the amounts spent being rendered, the amount spent is reimbursed to the holder. This restores the imprest to its fixed amount for meeting further petty works expenditure.

q: In the control of works expenditure, an allotment of funds, as distinguished from an appropriation, means:

options.A: The amount voted by Parliament for a grant as a whole
options.B: The distribution of the amount placed at disposal under a grant among the spending authorities for incurring expenditure
options.C: The sanction accorded to the detailed estimate of a work
options.D: The regularisation of excess expenditure after the close of the year

e: Allotment is the distribution of the amount placed at disposal under a grant among the spending authorities for incurring expenditure. Appropriation is the amount voted by Parliament for the grant as a whole, from which allotments are made.

q: Expenditure on works which is found, after the close of the financial year, to have exceeded the grant voted for the year is brought to notice and regularised through:

options.A: A note recorded in the Works Register of the division
options.B: The Contractor's Ledger maintained in the accounts office
options.C: The Appropriation Accounts, the excess being regularised by Parliament by voting an excess grant
options.D: The completion report of the work concerned alone

e: Excess expenditure over the grant voted for a year is disclosed in the Appropriation Accounts. It is regularised by Parliament by voting an excess grant, as required by the financial control procedure of the Railways.

q: A work involving expenditure of a nature not contemplated in the budget estimates of the year, which is required to be brought to the notice of Parliament, is treated as:

options.A: A minor work
options.B: A deposit work
options.C: A work charged to the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.D: A New Service / New Instrument of Service

e: Expenditure of a nature not contemplated in the budget estimates, which must be brought to the notice of Parliament, is treated as a New Service or New Instrument of Service. It cannot be incurred merely as a minor work or charged to a fund to avoid such notice.

q: The provision under the correct head of allocation for a work is exhausted, while funds are available under a wrong head. The correct course in booking the expenditure on the work is that:

options.A: The expenditure must be booked to the head under which funds happen to be available
options.B: The expenditure must be booked under its correct allocation, irrespective of the availability of budget provision, the provision being arranged separately
options.C: The expenditure must be held under a suspense head permanently
options.D: The work must be stopped in all cases until the next year's budget

e: Expenditure must always be booked under its correct head of allocation, irrespective of where budget provision happens to be available. Provision under the correct head is arranged separately; booking to a wrong head merely because funds exist there is a serious irregularity.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Extra Budgetary Resources (Institutional Finance) for railway projects are raised through market borrowings, mainly through the Indian Railway Finance Corporation.
2. Gross Budgetary Support received for the capital programme is itself a part of such market borrowings.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only is correct. Extra Budgetary Resources are market borrowings raised mainly through IRFC for railway projects. Gross Budgetary Support is budgetary support from the general exchequer, not itself a market borrowing, so statement 2 is wrong.

q: During the execution of a work, its estimated cost rises so much that the total cost now exceeds the powers of the authority which sanctioned the original estimate. The revised estimate of the work is required to be sanctioned by:

options.A: The original sanctioning authority itself in all cases
options.B: The Engineer-in-charge of the work
options.C: The authority competent to sanction an estimate of the total revised cost of the work
options.D: The tender committee which accepted the tender for the work

e: Where the revised cost of a work exceeds the powers of the authority that sanctioned the original estimate, the revised estimate must be sanctioned by the authority competent to sanction an estimate of the total revised cost. The original authority cannot sanction beyond its own powers.

q: On a work nearing completion, savings are anticipated under its sanctioned estimate. The executive proposes to use those savings for an altogether new item of work in another work of the division, without any fresh sanction. This course is:

options.A: Permissible, as the total allotment of the division is not exceeded
options.B: Permissible, if the Finance branch is informed after the event
options.C: Permissible, only for items costing very small amounts
options.D: Not permissible, as savings of one work cannot be utilised for another work or for new items without the sanction of the competent authority

e: Savings anticipated under one work's sanctioned estimate cannot be used for another work or for altogether new items without the sanction of the competent authority. The course proposed is not permissible merely because the divisional allotment as a whole is not exceeded.

q: A division finds that the allotment made for a work is not likely to be utilised during the year because the work has not progressed as expected. The division should:

options.A: Surrender the funds expected to remain unutilised promptly, so that they can be allotted for other purposes
options.B: Retain the allotment till March and spend it on any other work
options.C: Transfer the allotment to the staff welfare activities of the division
options.D: Book fictitious expenditure to keep the allotment alive

e: Funds allotted for a work that are not likely to be utilised during the year should be surrendered promptly. Surrender lets the funds be allotted for other purposes; retaining them till March or diverting them to other works or fictitious booking is irregular.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The sanction of an estimate of a work does not, by itself, authorise the incurring of expenditure on it unless funds for the purpose have been allotted.
2. The allotment of funds for a work dispenses with the need for sanction of its estimate by the competent authority.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only is correct. Sanction of an estimate does not by itself authorise incurring expenditure unless funds are allotted for it. But allotment of funds does not dispense with estimate sanction, so statement 2 is wrong.

q: A special machine is purchased exclusively for the execution of one particular bridge work and will have no general use in the division after that work. The cost of the machine is chargeable to:

options.A: The general tools and plant head of the division
options.B: The Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.C: The cost of that work itself
options.D: The contractor executing the bridge work in all cases

e: A special machine bought exclusively for one particular work and of no general use afterwards is charged to the cost of that work itself. It is not charged to the general tools and plant head, which covers plant of general divisional use.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The cost of surveys and investigations carried out for a work which is actually executed forms part of the cost of that work.
2. The cost of surveys and investigations carried out for a proposed work which is finally abandoned is written off to Revenue.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct. Survey and investigation cost of a work actually executed forms part of that work's cost, while the cost of surveys for a proposed work finally abandoned is written off to Revenue.

q: Land is acquired for a doubling project and compensation is paid for it. The cost of the land so acquired is:

options.A: Charged to Revenue as a maintenance expense
options.B: Held permanently under a suspense head
options.C: Borne by the State Government in all cases
options.D: Charged to the same head and fund as the project for which it is acquired, forming part of the cost of that project

e: Land acquired for a project, including compensation paid for it, is charged to the same head and fund as the project itself. The land cost forms part of the total cost of the doubling project and is not charged to Revenue or borne by the State Government.

q: An entry recorded in a Measurement Book is found to contain a mistake. The mistake is correctly set right by:

options.A: Striking out the wrong entry, writing the correction, and attesting it with the initials and date of the official making the correction
options.B: Erasing the original entry and writing the correct figures in its place
options.C: Tearing out the page of the book containing the entry
options.D: Overwriting the figures so that the original entry cannot be read

e: A mistake in a Measurement Book entry is corrected by striking out the wrong entry, writing the correction, and attesting it with the initials and date of the official making it. Erasures, overwriting and tearing out pages are prohibited, as the Measurement Book is a basic payment record.

q: A senior engineering official test-checks, on a sample basis, the measurements of a work recorded by a junior official in the Measurement Book. The object of this test check is to:

options.A: Re-measure the whole of the work done by the contractor
options.B: Delay the preparation of the contractor's running bill
options.C: Verify that the measurements recorded are correct
options.D: Fix the rates payable for the items of work executed

e: Test check of measurements by a senior official, on a sample basis, verifies that the measurements recorded by the junior official in the Measurement Book are correct. It is a supervisory check, not a complete re-measurement of the whole work.

q: Before a contractor's running bill for a work is prepared, the quantities of the items of work measured in the Measurement Book are summarised item-wise. This summary, on which the bill is based, is known as:

options.A: The comparative statement of tenders
options.B: The deviation statement of the work
options.C: The abstract of measurements
options.D: The briefing note for the tender committee

e: The item-wise summary of quantities measured in the Measurement Book, on which the contractor's running bill is prepared, is the abstract of measurements. The bill rates are applied to the quantities in this abstract.

q: The balance shown in the Material-at-Site account of a work is verified, for the purpose of its reconciliation, primarily by:

options.A: Comparing it with the balances in the Contractor's Ledger
options.B: Physical verification of the materials actually lying at the site of the work
options.C: Reference to the allotment shown against the work in the Pink Book
options.D: Checking the tender documents of the work

e: The Material-at-Site account balance of a work is reconciled primarily by physical verification of the materials actually lying at the site. The verified quantities are compared with the account balance and differences are investigated and adjusted.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Contractor's Ledger shows, contractor-wise, the bills passed, the advances made, the recoveries effected and the balance payable.
2. The Works Register shows, contractor-wise, the leave and attendance position of the labour engaged on works.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only is correct. The Contractor's Ledger shows contractor-wise the bills passed, advances made, recoveries effected and the balance payable. The Works Register does not show leave and attendance of labour, so statement 2 is wrong.

q: In the accounts office, the sanctions accorded by the competent authorities to estimates and to expenditure are recorded, for the purpose of internal check of works transactions, in the:

options.A: Hindrance Register
options.B: Register of Sanctions
options.C: Site Order Book
options.D: Encroachment Register

e: Sanctions accorded by competent authorities to estimates and expenditure are recorded in the Register of Sanctions maintained in the accounts office. It supports the internal check of works transactions against the authority under which expenditure was incurred.

q: The Revenue Allocation Register maintained in the accounts office serves the purpose of:

options.A: Checking that the expenditure on works and repairs is borne by the correct allocation, such as Capital, Depreciation Reserve Fund, Development Fund or Revenue
options.B: Listing the tenders received for works during the year
options.C: Recording the attendance of the staff of the accounts office
options.D: Recording the measurements of work done by contractors

e: The Revenue Allocation Register checks that expenditure on works and repairs is borne by the correct allocation, such as Capital, Depreciation Reserve Fund, Development Fund or Revenue. Correct allocation is essential because the source of funds and accounting treatment differ for each.

q: An amount paid in connection with a work, which is recoverable from an outside party, is initially debited to Miscellaneous Works Advances. A debit balance under this head accordingly represents:

options.A: Compensation paid to contractors for delay in completion of works
options.B: Amounts outstanding for recovery or adjustment in connection with works
options.C: The profit earned by the Railways on deposit works
options.D: The value of materials lying at the sites of works

e: Amounts paid in connection with a work that are recoverable from an outside party are debited to Miscellaneous Works Advances. A debit balance under this head therefore represents amounts outstanding for recovery or adjustment in connection with works.

q: The expenditure figures for a work recorded in the Works Register of the executive office differ from the figures booked for the same work in the accounts office. The correct treatment of the difference is that:

options.A: The figures are reconciled periodically between the two offices, so that the difference is noticed and set right
options.B: The difference is ignored, as the two records serve different purposes
options.C: The accounts office figures are altered to agree with the executive figures without any check
options.D: The difference is written off at the end of the year

e: Differences between Works Register figures of the executive office and the booked figures of the accounts office must be reconciled periodically between the two offices. Reconciliation brings the difference to notice and gets it set right; it is never ignored or written off without check.

q: A contractor's bill for a works contract is being passed for payment. In respect of the amounts payable to the contractor, the Railways are required to:

options.A: Deduct income tax at source, as required under the Income-tax Act, and deposit it with the Income-tax authorities
options.B: Deduct a contribution towards the contractor's own provident fund
options.C: Retain a part of every bill permanently as earnings of the Railways
options.D: Deduct the wages payable to the contractor's workmen for the next month

e: While passing a contractor's bill, the Railways must deduct income tax at source as required under the Income-tax Act and deposit it with the income-tax authorities. TDS is a statutory obligation on payments made under works contracts.

q: Earth and other minor minerals consumed in a work are subject to royalty or seigniorage charges payable to the State Government. Where such charges are leviable, they are ordinarily:

options.A: Borne by the workmen engaged on the work
options.B: Adjusted against the departmental charges of the work
options.C: Borne by the Railways without any recovery
options.D: Recovered from the contractor's bills at the applicable rates

e: Royalty or seigniorage charges on earth and minor minerals consumed in a work, payable to the State Government, are ordinarily recovered from the contractor's bills at the applicable rates where leviable. The contractor thus bears the charge for the material he consumes.

q: The departmental charges recovered from an outside party on a deposit work executed for that party are:

options.A: Retained by the executing division as its own funds
options.B: Credited to the earnings (revenue receipts) of the Railways
options.C: Deposited in the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.D: Refunded to the party on completion of the work

e: Departmental charges recovered from an outside party on a deposit work are credited to the earnings, that is revenue receipts, of the Railways. They are not retained by the division as its funds or refunded to the party.

q: A tenderer submits his tender subject to an additional condition of his own which materially departs from the conditions prescribed in the tender documents. Such a tender is treated as:

options.A: The lowest tender for the work
options.B: A tender which must be accepted after negotiation
options.C: A non-responsive tender, liable to be rejected
options.D: A tender which the tender committee must regularise

e: A tender submitted with an additional condition of the tenderer's own which materially departs from the prescribed tender conditions is a non-responsive tender. Under the GFR and GCC principles it is liable to be rejected, not accepted or regularised.

q: In a works tender, the pattern of the offers received gives reasonable ground to suspect that the tenderers have formed a cartel and indulged in bid-rigging. The proper course is that:

options.A: The lowest tender must still be accepted in all cases
options.B: The tender committee must negotiate with the cartel as a whole
options.C: Only a warning is issued and the tender is processed as usual
options.D: The tenders are liable to be rejected and action taken against the firms concerned in accordance with the procurement rules

e: Where the pattern of offers reasonably suggests cartel formation or bid-rigging, the tenders are liable to be rejected and action taken against the firms under the procurement rules. The lowest tender is not accepted mechanically in such a case.

q: A material change in the conditions of a tender is issued by a corrigendum only a few days before the due date fixed for submission of tenders. In such a case:

options.A: The due date for submission is suitably extended, so that the tenderers get adequate time to take the change into account
options.B: The due date remains unchanged in all cases
options.C: The tenders already received are opened at once
options.D: The tender is cancelled in all cases

e: When a material change is issued by corrigendum only a few days before the due date, the date for submission of tenders is suitably extended. Tenderers must get adequate time to take the change into account in their bids, as required by fair procurement practice under the GFR.

q: In response to an open tender for a work, only one valid offer is received. In such a case:

options.A: The single tenderer must be awarded the work at his quoted rates without any examination
options.B: The tender must invariably be discharged and fresh tenders invited, whatever the rates quoted
options.C: The single offer may be considered for acceptance if the rates are reasonable, with the approval of the competent authority and the concurrence of Finance
options.D: The work must be executed departmentally in all such cases

e: A single valid offer received against an open tender may be considered for acceptance if the rates are reasonable, with the approval of the competent authority and the concurrence of Finance. It is neither awarded automatically nor invariably discharged.

q: While examining the rates quoted in the tenders received for a work, the tender committee ordinarily judges the reasonableness of the rates by comparing them with:

options.A: The rates proposed by the contractor in his earlier correspondence
options.B: The personal assessment of the sectional staff
options.C: The Last Accepted Rates for similar works and the applicable schedule of rates
options.D: The rates quoted in the tenders of an adjoining Railway only

e: The tender committee judges the reasonableness of quoted rates mainly by comparing them with the Last Accepted Rates for similar works and the applicable schedule of rates. These are the accepted benchmarks for rate reasonableness in works tenders.

q: After the tenders for a work have been opened, it is found that the lowest tenderer does not fulfil an eligibility criterion laid down in the tender documents. The criterion:

options.A: Can be relaxed in his favour by the Engineer-in-charge
options.B: Can be modified by the tender committee to suit his case
options.C: Is applicable only to Government undertakings
options.D: Cannot be relaxed or changed after the opening of tenders

e: An eligibility criterion laid down in the tender documents cannot be relaxed or changed after the opening of tenders, even in favour of the lowest tenderer. Relaxation after opening would vitiate the tender process and is not within the powers of the Engineer-in-charge or the tender committee.

q: A works contract is being executed by a joint venture of firms. One member of the venture fails to perform its part of the obligations. As regards the liability towards the Railways:

options.A: Only the defaulting member can be proceeded against
options.B: The liability of the members is joint and several, so that every member is fully liable to the Railways for the obligations under the contract
options.C: The liability is borne by the Railways themselves
options.D: The liability is limited to the lead member's share in the profit of the work

e: In a joint venture, the liability of the members towards the Railways is joint and several. Every member is fully liable for the obligations under the contract, so the Railways are not confined to proceeding only against the defaulting member.

q: In the terminology of the General Financial Rules, the earnest money which a bidder is required to furnish along with his bid for a work is referred to as:

options.A: Retention money
options.B: Performance security
options.C: Bid security
options.D: Tender deposit

e: Under the General Financial Rules, the earnest money furnished by a bidder along with his bid is termed bid security. Performance security is furnished later by the successful bidder for due performance of the contract.

q: The amount charged to a tenderer towards the cost of the tender documents of a work is:

options.A: Refunded to all tenderers after the tender is decided
options.B: Adjusted against the earnest money of every tenderer
options.C: Refunded only to the successful tenderer
options.D: Not refundable, whether or not his tender is accepted

e: The amount charged towards the cost of tender documents is not refundable, whether or not the tenderer's bid is accepted. It is neither refunded to all tenderers nor adjusted against earnest money.

q: A tenderer who has submitted his bid in e-tendering through IREPS wishes to withdraw the bid. He can do so:

options.A: At any time before the due date and time fixed for submission of bids
options.B: At any time before the work is awarded to him
options.C: Only after the tenders are opened
options.D: Only with the permission of the tender committee

e: In e-tendering through IREPS, a bidder can withdraw his bid at any time before the due date and time fixed for submission of bids. After that deadline the bid cannot be withdrawn at will.

q: Tenders invited by Government organisations, including the Railways, are, in accordance with the General Financial Rules, also required to be published on:

options.A: The website of the concerned State Government only
options.B: The notice board of the nearest district court
options.C: The website of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.D: The Central Public Procurement Portal

e: Under the General Financial Rules, tenders invited by Government organisations including the Railways must also be published on the Central Public Procurement Portal. This ensures wide publicity and transparency of public procurement.

q: For some items of a tender, the rates quoted by a tenderer appear to be abnormally high or abnormally low in comparison with the schedule of rates. Before making its recommendation, the tender committee should:

options.A: Accept the rates without any examination
options.B: Substitute the schedule rates for those items on its own
options.C: Reject the tender in all cases
options.D: Examine the justification for such rates and may call upon the tenderer to justify them

e: Where quoted rates appear abnormally high or abnormally low compared with the schedule of rates, the tender committee should examine the justification for them and may call upon the tenderer to justify the rates before recommending. It does not substitute schedule rates on its own or accept blindly.

q: Unless the contract otherwise provides, a works contractor is required, at his own cost, to provide:

options.A: Only the supervisory staff for the work
options.B: All labour, materials, tools and plant and everything necessary for the execution of the work
options.C: Only the transport for departmental materials
options.D: Only the materials for the work

e: Unless the contract otherwise provides, the contractor must provide at his own cost all labour, materials, tools and plant and everything necessary for execution of the work. This is a basic obligation under the General Conditions of Contract for Works.

q: An arbitral award made in a dispute arising out of a works contract has not been set aside by any court. Unless set aside, such an award is:

options.A: Merely advisory in nature for the parties
options.B: Binding only if the contractor agrees to it
options.C: Enforceable in the same manner as a decree of a court
options.D: Valid only for one year from the date of the award

e: An arbitral award that has not been set aside by a court is enforceable in the same manner as a decree of a court, under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. It is not merely advisory and does not need the contractor's agreement to bind the parties.

q: Owing to unprecedented floods, a force majeure event beyond the control of the parties, the execution of a work remains suspended for a considerable period. The consequence under the contract is that:

options.A: The contractor forfeits his security deposit for the period of suspension
options.B: The period of completion is suitably extended and neither party is liable for damages in respect of the delay so caused
options.C: Liquidated damages are levied on the contractor for the whole period
options.D: The contract stands automatically determined

e: Where a force majeure event such as unprecedented floods suspends execution, the completion period is suitably extended and neither party is liable for damages for the delay so caused, under the force majeure provisions of the GCC. Liquidated damages are not levied for such a period.

q: The insurance policies taken out by a contractor for a work under the General Conditions of Contract are required to be in the joint names of:

options.A: The contractor and his bank
options.B: The contractor and the Engineer personally
options.C: The Railways and the contractor
options.D: The contractor and his sub-contractor

e: Insurance policies taken out by the contractor for the work under the GCC must be in the joint names of the Railways and the contractor. This protects the Railways' interest in the insured work and materials along with the contractor's.

q: On the orders of the Engineer, a portion of work already executed and covered up is opened up for inspection and testing, and the work is found to conform to the contract. The cost of such opening up, testing and reinstatement is borne by:

options.A: The contractor in all cases
options.B: The Railways
options.C: The tender committee
options.D: The contractor and the Railways in equal shares

e: Where work opened up for inspection on the Engineer's orders is found to conform to the contract, the cost of opening up, testing and reinstatement is borne by the Railways, under the GCC provision on uncovering work. Had the work been defective, the contractor would have borne it.

q: A contractor anticipates that he will not be able to complete a work by the stipulated date and wishes to apply for extension of the period of completion. His application should ordinarily be made:

options.A: Only after the final bill of the work is paid
options.B: At any time within one year after the completion of the work
options.C: To the tender committee which recommended his tender
options.D: Before the expiry of the stipulated date of completion of the work

e: An application for extension of the completion period should ordinarily be made before the expiry of the stipulated date of completion. Applying in time lets the Engineer consider the extension while the contract period is still current, as contemplated by the GCC.

q: A contractor raises, for the first time long after the event, a claim for extra payment under a contract, without having notified the claim to the Engineer within the period stipulated in the contract. The claim:

options.A: Must be paid at the schedule of rates in all cases
options.B: May be treated as waived, as provided in the contract
options.C: Automatically extends the period of completion of the work
options.D: Is decided by the tender committee in favour of the contractor

e: A claim for extra payment raised long after the event, without notice to the Engineer within the period stipulated in the contract, may be treated as waived under the contract. The GCC notice requirement bars stale claims not notified in time.

q: Plant and machinery brought to the site by a contractor, against which an advance for plant and machinery has been paid to him, stand:

options.A: As the unencumbered property of the contractor, removable by him at will
options.B: Sold to the Railways from the date of the advance
options.C: Treated as materials consumed in the work
options.D: Hypothecated to the Railways, and cannot be removed from the site without the permission of the Engineer

e: Plant and machinery brought to site against which a plant and machinery advance has been paid stand hypothecated to the Railways. The contractor cannot remove them from the site without the Engineer's permission until the advance is recovered.

q: In a staircase of a building, the 'tread' of a step is:

options.A: The horizontal upper surface of the step, on which the foot rests while ascending or descending
options.B: The vertical face of the step, whose height is the rise of the step
options.C: The sloping member which supports the steps of the staircase
options.D: The protective railing provided along the open side of the staircase

e: The tread of a step is its horizontal upper surface, on which the foot rests while ascending or descending the staircase. The vertical face of the step, whose height is the rise, is the riser.
